guided.title: Left merge keeps all orders
guided.prompt: Merge `orders` with `customers` on `customer_id`, keeping every order. Print the merged table with `print(m.to_string(index=False))`; the columns are `order_id`, `customer_id`, `amount`, `name`.
guided.starter:
import pandas as pd
customers = pd.DataFrame({"customer_id": [1, 2], "name": ["Ada", "Bo"]})
orders = pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [10, 11, 12], "customer_id": [1, 2, 3], "amount": [5, 6, 7]})
print(orders.to_string(index=False))
guided.solution:
import pandas as pd
customers = pd.DataFrame({"customer_id": [1, 2], "name": ["Ada", "Bo"]})
orders = pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [10, 11, 12], "customer_id": [1, 2, 3], "amount": [5, 6, 7]})
m = orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left")
print(m.to_string(index=False))
hints: The orders table is the main table, so it goes on the left.
`how="left"` keeps every left row and fills `NaN` where there is no match.
guided.expected:
order_id  customer_id  amount name
       10            1       5  Ada
       11            2       6   Bo
       12            3       7  NaN

guided.title: Row counts by join type
guided.prompt: Merge `a` and `b` on `k` with each of `inner`, `left`, `right` and `outer`. Print four lines of the form `how rows`, for example `inner 2`, in that order.
guided.starter:
import pandas as pd
a = pd.DataFrame({"k": [1, 2, 3], "x": ["p", "q", "r"]})
b = pd.DataFrame({"k": [2, 3, 4, 5], "y": ["s", "t", "u", "v"]})
print(len(a), len(b))
guided.solution:
import pandas as pd
a = pd.DataFrame({"k": [1, 2, 3], "x": ["p", "q", "r"]})
b = pd.DataFrame({"k": [2, 3, 4, 5], "y": ["s", "t", "u", "v"]})
for how in ["inner", "left", "right", "outer"]:
    print(how, len(a.merge(b, on="k", how=how)))
hints: Loop over the four join names and merge with `how=how` each time.
Print the join name and `len` of the merged table.
`print(how, len(a.merge(b, on="k", how=how)))` inside the loop.

guided.title: Different key names
guided.prompt: `orders` has the key `cust` and `people` has the key `id`. Merge them (inner join) and drop the redundant `id` column. Print `print(m.to_string(index=False))`; columns `order_id`, `cust`, `name`.
guided.starter:
import pandas as pd
orders = pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [1, 2, 3], "cust": [10, 20, 10]})
people = pd.DataFrame({"id": [10, 20], "name": ["Ada", "Bo"]})
print(orders.to_string(index=False))
guided.solution:
import pandas as pd
orders = pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [1, 2, 3], "cust": [10, 20, 10]})
people = pd.DataFrame({"id": [10, 20], "name": ["Ada", "Bo"]})
m = orders.merge(people, left_on="cust", right_on="id").drop(columns="id")
print(m.to_string(index=False))
hints: When the key names differ, `on` cannot be used.
Use `left_on` for the left table's column and `right_on` for the right table's.
After the merge, `drop(columns="id")` removes the extra key column.
guided.expected:
order_id  cust name
        1    10  Ada
        2    20   Bo
        3    10  Ada

guided.title: Customers who never ordered
guided.prompt: Find the names of customers with no orders using a left merge from `customers` to `orders` with `indicator=True`. Print the names as a list with `print(names)`, in the order of the customers table.
guided.starter:
import pandas as pd
customers = pd.DataFrame({"customer_id": [1, 2, 3, 4], "name": ["Ada", "Bo", "Cy", "Di"]})
orders = pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [1, 2], "customer_id": [2, 4]})
print(customers["name"].tolist())
guided.solution:
import pandas as pd
customers = pd.DataFrame({"customer_id": [1, 2, 3, 4], "name": ["Ada", "Bo", "Cy", "Di"]})
orders = pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [1, 2], "customer_id": [2, 4]})
m = customers.merge(orders, on="customer_id", how="left", indicator=True)
names = m[m["_merge"] == "left_only"]["name"].tolist()
print(names)
hints: A left merge from customers keeps customers without orders.
`indicator=True` adds a `_merge` column; unmatched left rows are `left_only`.

independent.title: Revenue by city with checks
independent.prompt: Merge `orders` with `customers` (left join, `validate="many_to_one"`), then total `amount` per `city`, treating orders with no customer as the city `"unknown"` (use `fillna`). Print the totals with `print(totals.to_string())` sorted by city, then print `True` or `False` for whether the total of the city totals equals the total of the original orders.
independent.starter:
import pandas as pd
customers = pd.DataFrame({"customer_id": [1, 2, 3], "city": ["Oslo", "Rome", "Oslo"]})
orders = pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], "customer_id": [1, 2, 3, 1, 9], "amount": [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]})
print(orders["amount"].sum())
independent.solution:
import pandas as pd
customers = pd.DataFrame({"customer_id": [1, 2, 3], "city": ["Oslo", "Rome", "Oslo"]})
orders = pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], "customer_id": [1, 2, 3, 1, 9], "amount": [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]})
m = orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left", validate="many_to_one")
m["city"] = m["city"].fillna("unknown")
totals = m.groupby("city")["amount"].sum()
print(totals.to_string())
print(totals.sum() == orders["amount"].sum())

independent.title: Reconcile two systems
independent.prompt: Two systems list order ids: `src` (source) and `wh` (warehouse), each with an `order_id` and an `amount`. Outer-merge them on `order_id` with the indicator and `suffixes=("_src", "_wh")`. Print three lines: ids only in the source (sorted list), ids only in the warehouse (sorted list), and the sorted list of ids present in both whose amounts differ.
independent.starter:
import pandas as pd
src = pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [1, 2, 3, 4], "amount": [10, 20, 30, 40]})
wh = pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [2, 3, 4, 5], "amount": [20, 35, 40, 50]})
print(len(src), len(wh))
independent.solution:
import pandas as pd
src = pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [1, 2, 3, 4], "amount": [10, 20, 30, 40]})
wh = pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [2, 3, 4, 5], "amount": [20, 35, 40, 50]})
m = src.merge(wh, on="order_id", how="outer", indicator=True, suffixes=("_src", "_wh"))
print(sorted(m[m["_merge"] == "left_only"]["order_id"].tolist()))
print(sorted(m[m["_merge"] == "right_only"]["order_id"].tolist()))
both = m[m["_merge"] == "both"]
print(sorted(both[both["amount_src"] != both["amount_wh"]]["order_id"].tolist()))

independent.title: Stretch: find the duplicate key
independent.prompt: The lookup table `prices` has a duplicated `sku`. Merging it with `lines` changes the row count and the revenue. Print four lines: rows in `lines`, rows after a left merge, the list of duplicated skus (sorted), and the number of rows after merging with a de-duplicated lookup (`drop_duplicates(subset="sku")`) using `validate="many_to_one"`.
independent.starter:
import pandas as pd
lines = pd.DataFrame({"line": [1, 2, 3, 4], "sku": ["a", "b", "a", "c"]})
prices = pd.DataFrame({"sku": ["a", "b", "b", "c"], "price": [5, 7, 7, 9]})
print(len(lines))
independent.solution:
import pandas as pd
lines = pd.DataFrame({"line": [1, 2, 3, 4], "sku": ["a", "b", "a", "c"]})
prices = pd.DataFrame({"sku": ["a", "b", "b", "c"], "price": [5, 7, 7, 9]})
print(len(lines))
print(len(lines.merge(prices, on="sku", how="left")))
print(sorted(prices[prices["sku"].duplicated()]["sku"].unique().tolist()))
clean = prices.drop_duplicates(subset="sku")
print(len(lines.merge(clean, on="sku", how="left", validate="many_to_one")))

checks.question: `orders` has 5 rows; one has a customer id missing from `customers`. How many rows does `orders.merge(customers, on='customer_id')` return, assuming unique customer ids?
checks.explanation: The default is an inner join, so the unmatched order is dropped and 4 rows remain. `how="left"` would keep all 5. No error is raised for missing matches.

checks.question: The customers key is duplicated for one customer with 2 orders. After `orders.merge(customers, on='customer_id', how='left')`, what happens to that customer's orders?
options: Nothing, left joins never add rows
They are merged into one row
checks.explanation: Each order matches both duplicate customer rows, so it appears twice and revenue is inflated. A left join only guarantees no left row is lost; `validate="many_to_one"` would raise an error.

checks.question: Which `_merge` value marks a customer who exists only in the left table of an outer merge?
checks.explanation: `left_only` means the key was present in the left table only. `right_only` is the reverse and `both` means both tables had the key. `unmatched` is not a value pandas uses.

checks.question: `a` has keys [1, 2, 3] and `b` has keys [2, 3, 4, 5], all unique. What are the row counts for inner, left, right and outer?
checks.explanation: Inner keeps keys 2 and 3: 2 rows. Left keeps all 3 of `a`. Right keeps all 4 of `b`. Outer keeps the union {1,2,3,4,5}: 5 rows, not 7, because matching keys share one row.

checks.question: Both tables have a non-key column `name`. What are the columns in the merged result when `suffixes` is not given?
options: name only, from the left table
checks.explanation: Pandas keeps both columns and appends `_x` to the left and `_y` to the right. It never silently drops one. Pass `suffixes` to choose meaningful names.
